Game caught by one's trained dog sent with Allah's name may be eaten, unless the dog ate from it or another dog joined the hunt.
Muhrims may eat game hunted by Abu Qatada, not in ihram, if none prompted or pointed it out; the Prophet returned a gifted onager since he was in ihram.
Abu Qatada, not in Ihram, killed an onager that his companions in Ihram would not help him hunt, and the Prophet, in Ihram, ate the foreleg he had kept.
The Prophet accepted and ate the thighs of a rabbit Anas caught, but declined an onager presented while he was in Ihram, explaining this to the saddened giver.
The Prophet declined As-Sa'b's gift of onager meat at Al-Abwa' or Waddan because he was in Ihram, and told the saddened giver so.
Game killed by a Mi'rad's edge or a trained hound sent with Allah's name may be eaten, not if struck by its side or another dog joined; stone-throwing hunts nothing.
Game a trained hound sent with Allah's name catches is lawful unless it ate or other hounds joined; arrow-shot game found days later may be eaten unless in water.
Anas caught a rabbit whose legs the Prophet accepted; Abu Qatada, not in Ihram, killed an onager alone, and the Prophet told companions in Ihram it was food from Allah.
The Prophet forbade flicking stones with the fingers, which neither hunts game nor hurts an enemy but gouges out an eye or breaks a tooth.
